lesson.title: Rising From the Ashes: Secondary Succession After Disturbance
lesson.summary: Secondary succession is the type of ecological succession that begins in a place where soil already exists after a disturbance has removed most or all of the community, such as after a fire or the abandonment of farmland, and it typically proceeds much faster than primary succession.
lesson.body:
Secondary succession is ecological succession that begins where soil is already present, following a disturbance that removed or severely damaged the existing community without destroying the soil itself. A wildfire that burns through a forest, a hurricane that flattens trees, or a farm field that is plowed for decades and then abandoned are all common starting points. In every one of these cases, the ground underneath still contains soil, along with at least some seeds, roots, and microorganisms left over from before the disturbance, which is the key difference from primary succession and the reason secondary succession moves so much faster.

Old field succession on abandoned farmland is one of the most thoroughly studied examples of secondary succession, particularly in regions of the eastern United States where farmland has been left fallow and observed over subsequent decades. The general pattern that tends to emerge is a shift from fast growing annual weeds in the first year or two, since these are quick to sprout from wind blown or soil banked seeds, toward longer lived perennial grasses and herbaceous plants over the next several years, then toward shrubs and fast growing, sun loving tree species such as pines over a decade or two, and eventually, over several more decades, toward a more shade tolerant hardwood forest as those hardwood species grow up underneath and eventually outcompete the pines for light. The exact species involved differ by region and climate, but this broad trajectory, from fast, short lived colonizers toward slower growing, longer lived, more shade tolerant species, is a recurring feature of secondary succession in many temperate ecosystems.

Forest regrowth after a wildfire follows a related but somewhat different path, depending heavily on how severe the fire was. Because soil nutrients, seed banks, and even resprouting root systems frequently survive a fire, vegetation can begin returning within the very first growing season afterward, in the form of grasses, wildflowers, and resprouting shrubs. Some tree species have even evolved traits specifically suited to fire, such as cones that only release their seeds after being exposed to intense heat, which allows those species to reestablish quickly on a freshly burned landscape. Over subsequent years and decades, shrubs and young trees fill in, and the forest gradually rebuilds toward something resembling its earlier structure, though the exact pace and outcome depend on fire severity, climate, and which species were present nearby to reseed the area.

Compared to primary succession, which can take centuries because it must start by building soil from bare rock, secondary succession on already soiled ground can visibly transform a landscape within just years to a few decades, precisely because so much of the biological foundation, the soil, the seed bank, and often surviving roots, is already in place before the process even begins. Both forms of succession, primary and secondary, illustrate the same broader idea introduced two chapters ago: communities are not fixed and permanent, they are dynamic, and given enough time and freedom from further major disturbance, they tend to move from simpler, less diverse states toward richer, more complex ones.
